questions.stem:
A researcher is investigating the growth of two types of tree, Birch and Maple. The height, to the nearest cm, a seedling grows in one year is recorded for 35 Birch trees and 32 Maple trees. The results are summarised in the back-to-back stem and leaf diagram below.

Totals   Birch                    Maple   Totals
(2)         9 8 | 2 | 5 7 7 8 9      (5)
(8)   9 9 9 6 5 3 1 1 | 3 | 0 2 6 6 8 9 9   (7)
(9)   9 8 8 7 6 3 1 1 1 | 4 | 1 1 1 $k$ 7 8   (6)
(9)   7 7 7 5 4 3 2 1 0 | 5 | 0 1 2 3 4 4 4   (7)
(3)               7 6 5 | 6 | 3 4 6         (3)
(3)               6 5 4 | 7 | 0 7           (2)
(1)                   5 | 8 | 0 0           (2)

Key: 5 | 6 | 3 means 65 cm for a Birch tree and 63 cm for a Maple tree

The median height that these Maple trees grow in one year is 45 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the value of $k$, used in the stem and leaf diagram.
(1)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find the lower quartile and the upper quartile of the height grown in one year for these Birch trees.
(2)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The researcher defines an outlier as an observation that is

greater than $Q_3+1.5\times(Q_3-Q_1)$ or less than $Q_1-1.5\times(Q_3-Q_1)$

(c) Show that there is only one outlier amongst the Birch trees.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: "57"$+1.5\times$("57"$-$"39") or "39"$-1.5\times$("57"$-$"39")
A1: 84 and 12 therefore only 1 outlier [85]
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for either method correct or a correct value (ft their $Q_1$ and their $Q_3$)
- A1 Both limits for outliers correct and statement about the outlier or the outlier given.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
The grid on page 3 shows a box plot for the heights that the Maple trees grow in one year.

(d) On the same grid draw a box plot for the heights that the Birch trees grow in one year.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: for a box drawn with only 2 whiskers, only one at each end (condone median line missing)
M1: for upper whisker ending at 76 (or 84 ft their upper outlier limit) and lower whisker ending at 28
M1: for $Q_1, Q_2$ and $Q_3$ plotted, with $Q_2=48$ and ft their $Q_1$ and $Q_3$
A1: for a fully correct box plot with the outlier correctly shown – must be only 1

parts.label: e
parts.text:
(e) Comment on any difference in the distributions of the growth of these Birch trees and the growth of these Maple trees.
State the values of any statistics you have used to support your comment.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1ft: A correct difference of the medians with supporting figures
e.g. On average Birch [trees grow slightly] taller as the median is larger 48 > 45 oe
or
A correct difference of the spread with supporting figures
e.g. Maple has a greater spread/variation of heights as the range is larger 55 > 48 (excluding outlier) oe
e.g. Birch has a greater spread/variation of heights as the range is larger 57 > 55 (with outlier) oe
Official notes (completeness pass):
- for a correct comment, referring to heights, with reference to a correctly named statistic. Must include the figures compared. Allow 'grow more/bigger' to imply taller. Ignore any reference to skew
- SC If Q1/Q3 are incorrect then allow a ft comment about spread referring to the difference in IQR if compared to 18

parts.label: f
parts.text:
The researcher realises he has missed out 4 pieces of data for the Maple trees. The heights each seedling grows in one year, to the nearest cm, in ascending order, for these 4 Maple trees are 27 cm, $a$ cm, 48 cm, $2a$ cm.

Given that there is no change to the box plot for the Maple trees given on page 3

(f) find the range of possible values for $a$
Show your working clearly.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $36\leqslant a<x$ where $43\leqslant x\leqslant 45$ or $54\leqslant 2a\leqslant 80$
A1ft: $36\leqslant a\leqslant$"43" and $54\leqslant 2a\leqslant 80$
A1: $36\leqslant a\leqslant 40$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for either range correct. Allow $72\leqslant 2a\leqslant 80$ or $27\leqslant a\leqslant 40$ for $54\leqslant 2a\leqslant 80$. Condone < rather than $\leqslant$. May be seen as separate inequalities e.g. $2a\leqslant 80$, $2a\geqslant 54$ is allowed for $54\leqslant 2a\leqslant 80$. A final answer of $36\leqslant a\leqslant 40$ or $36<a<40$ implies M1
- A1ft for both ranges correct ft their k. Allow $72\leqslant 2a\leqslant 80$ or $27\leqslant a\leqslant 40$ for $54\leqslant 2a\leqslant 80$. Condone < rather than $\leqslant$. May be seen as separate inequalities
- A1 Allow 36 to 40 or 36, 37, 38, 39, 40. NB It is possible to get M1A0A1

questions.stem:
The lengths, $x$ mm, of 50 pebbles are summarised in the table below.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{Length} & \text{Frequency}\\ \hline 20\leqslant x<30 & 2\\ \hline 30\leqslant x<32 & 16\\ \hline 32\leqslant x<36 & 20\\ \hline 36\leqslant x<40 & 8\\ \hline 40\leqslant x<45 & 3\\ \hline 45\leqslant x<50 & 1\\ \hline\end{array}$

A histogram is drawn to represent these data.

The bar representing the class $32\leqslant x<36$ is 2.5 cm wide and 7.5 cm tall.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Calculate the width and the height of the bar representing the class $30\leqslant x<32$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Width = 1.25 [cm]
M1: $18.75$ cm$^2$ for freq of 20 so $\frac{18.75}{20}\times16=15$ cm$^2$ for a frequency of 16 or $w\times h=15$ or fd = 5
A1: [$h=15\div1.25$ or $h=8\div5\times7.5$ =] 12 (cm)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for sight of 15 or "their w"$\times$"their h"$=15$ or fd = 5 May be implied by h = 12

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Using linear interpolation, estimate the median of $x$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $Q_2=[32+]\frac{7}{20}\times4$ or using $n+1$ gives $Q_2=[32+]\frac{7.5}{20}\times4$
A1: $=33.4$ ($n+1$ gives 33.5)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for $\frac{7}{20}\times4$ or $\frac{13}{20}\times4$ or $\frac{m-32}{25-18}=\frac{4}{20}$ oe or $\frac{36-m}{38-25}=\frac{4}{20}$ oe (allow 25.5 rather than 25)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The weight, $w$ grams, of each of the 50 pebbles is coded using $10y=w-20$
These coded data are summarised by

$\sum y=104\qquad \sum y^2=233.54$

(c) Show that the mean of $w$ is 40.8
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $\bar{y}=\frac{104}{50}$[=2.08] or $\sum(w-20)=10\times104$[=1040] or $\sum w=10\times104+50\times20$[=2040]
A1*: $\bar{w}=10\times$"2.08"$+20=40.8$ or $\frac{\text{"1040"}}{50}+20=40.8$ or $\frac{\text{"2040"}}{50}=40.8$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for a correct method to find the mean of y or $\sum(w-20)$ or $\sum w$ ($10\times104+k$ where $k\neq20\times50$ is M0)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Calculate the standard deviation of $w$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: [Variance of $y$=]$\frac{233.54}{50}-(\text{"2.08"})^2$[=$\frac{861}{2500}=0.3444$] or $10\times$sd of $y=$sd of $w$ or $100\times233.54=\sum(w^2)-40\times$"2040"$+50\times400$[$\Rightarrow\sum(w^2)=84954$] oe
M1: [Variance of $w$=]"0.3444"$\times100$ or $\frac{\text{"84954"}}{50}-40.8^2$[=$\frac{861}{25}=34.44$]
M1: or sd of $y=\sqrt{\text{"0.3444"}}$[=$\frac{\sqrt{861}}{50}=0.5868...$]
sd of $w=\sqrt{\text{"0.3444"}\times100}$ or $\sqrt{\text{"34.44"}}$ or $10\times\text{"}\frac{\sqrt{861}}{50}\text{"}$
A1: $=5.868...$ awrt 5.87
Official notes (completeness pass):
- A1 awrt 5.87 NB an exact answer $\frac{\sqrt{861}}{5}$ scores A0

parts.label: e
parts.text:
The weight of a pebble recorded as 40.8 grams is added to the sample.

(e) Without carrying out any further calculations, state, giving a reason, what effect this would have on the value of

(i) the mean of $w$

(ii) the standard deviation of $w$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: (i) The mean would not change (as 40.8 is the mean)
B1: (ii) The standard deviation would decrease (as 40.8 is in the middle so data closer together)
ddB1: Both previous B1 awarded. For a correct reason for the sd decreasing. Allow $\sum(x-\bar{x})=0$. Allow $\sum(x-\bar{x})^2$ doesn't change and $n$ increases. Allow the values would be more concentrated about the mean
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1 for no change (No reason needed) Allow mean = 40.8 to imply no change
- B1 for sd decreases/be smaller/go down (condone Var decreases) (No reason needed)

questions.stem:
A competition consists of two rounds.

The time, in minutes, taken by adults to complete round one is modelled by a normal distribution with mean 15 minutes and standard deviation 2 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Use standardisation to find the proportion of adults that take less than 18 minutes to complete round one.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $\mathrm{P}(X<18)=\mathrm{P}\left(Z<\pm\left(\frac{18-15}{2}\right)\right)$[=$\pm1.5$]
A1: $=0.9332$ awrt 0.933
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for standardising correctly May be implied by $\pm1.5$. A1 awrt 0.933 (Do not ISW)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Only the fastest 60% of adults from round one take part in round two.

(b) Use standardisation to find the longest time that an adult can take to complete round one if they are to take part in round two.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1B1: $\frac{x-15}{2}=0.2533$
A1: $x=15.506...$ awrt 15.5
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for correct standardisation = to a z value such that $0.25\leqslant|z|\leqslant0.26$. B1 for use of awrt $\pm0.2533$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The time, $T$ minutes, taken by adults to complete round two is modelled by a normal distribution with mean $\mu$

Given that $\mathrm{P}(\mu-10<T<\mu+10)=0.95$

(c) find $\mathrm{P}(T>\mu-5\mid T>\mu-10)$
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $\mathrm{P}(T>\mu-10)=0.975$
M1: $\frac{(\mu\pm10)-\mu}{\sigma}=\pm1.96\Rightarrow\sigma=\frac{10}{1.96}$[=5.10...]
M1: $\mathrm{P}(T>\mu-5)=\mathrm{P}\left(Z>\frac{\mu-5-\mu}{\text{"5.10..."}}\right)$[=$-0.98$][=0.836...]
M1: $\mathrm{P}(T>\mu-5\mid T>\mu-10)=\frac{\text{"0.836..."}}{\text{"0.975"}}$
A1: $=0.8579...$ awrt 0.858
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for the correct probability of 0.975 – may be seen as the denominator of the fraction. May be implied by use of $|z|=1.96$ or better
- M1 For $\frac{\mu+10-\mu}{\sigma}=1.96$ or $\frac{\mu-10-\mu}{\sigma}=-1.96$, leading to a value for $\sigma$ May be implied by $\pm0.98$
- M1 for a correct method to find $\mathrm{P}(T>\mu-5)$ using their value for $\sigma$ May be implied by $-0.98$ If $\mathrm{P}(T<\mu+5)$ is calculated then this may be implied by 0.98
- M1 for $\frac{p}{0.975}$ where $0.5<p<0.975$ (must be a probability not their z value) If the denominator is incorrect only follow through their $\mathrm{P}(T>\mu-10)$ if clearly labelled and > 0.95

questions.stem:
The Venn diagram shows the probabilities related to teenagers playing 3 particular board games.

$C$ is the event that a teenager plays Chess
$S$ is the event that a teenager plays Scrabble
$G$ is the event that a teenager plays Go

where $p$ and $q$ are probabilities.

[Venn diagram: region $C$ only = 0.04; $C\cap G$ only = $p$; $G$ only = 0; $C\cap S$ only (not $G$) = 0.12; $C\cap S\cap G$ = 0.15; $S\cap G$ only (not $C$) = 0.1; $S$ only = 0.23; outside all three circles = $q$]

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that a randomly selected teenager plays Chess but does not play Go.
(1)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given that the events $C$ and $S$ are independent,

(b) find the value of $p$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
Mark parts (b) and (c) together. If values are given in the diagram and the script, then the script takes precedence.
M1: [$\mathrm{P}(C)=$]$0.04+0.15+0.12+p$[=0.31+p] or [$\mathrm{P}(C')=$]$0.1+0.23+q$[=0.33+q]
M1: [$\mathrm{P}(S)=$]$0.1+0.15+0.12+0.23$[=0.6] [$\mathrm{P}(S')=$]$1-(0.12+0.15+0.1+0.23)$[=0.4]; [$\mathrm{P}(S\cap C)=$]$0.15+0.12$[=0.27] [$\mathrm{P}(S'\cap C')=$]$q$
M1d: ("0.31"$+p)\times$"0.6"="0.27" oe or ("0.33"$+q)\times$"0.4"=$q$ oe
A1: $p=0.14$ oe or $q=0.22$ oe
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 all 3 correct probability expressions Allow P(C) = 0.45
- M1d dependent on the 1st M1 being awarded for use of $\mathrm{P}(C\cap S)=\mathrm{P}(C)\times\mathrm{P}(S)$ oe or $\mathrm{P}(C'\cap S')=\mathrm{P}(C')\times\mathrm{P}(S')$ ft their probabilities if labelled clearly

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Hence find the value of $q$
